articles.title: World Space Week 2026 Celebrates the “Rocket Revolution”
articles.author: World Space Week Association

paras.en: HOUSTON, Texas (September 30, 2026)— World Space Week events, beginning October 4 in 100 nations, will celebrate how launch innovation has stimulated the rapidly-growing space economy and enabled new uses of space to help the world.
paras.zh: 德克萨斯州休斯顿（2026 年 9 月 30 日）——世界太空周活动将于 10 月 4 日在 100 个国家开始，庆祝发射创新如何刺激快速增长的太空经济，并实现太空的新用途来帮助世界。

paras.en: “This year’s theme is the Rocket Revolution,” said Dennis Stone, World Space Week Association President. “It recognizes how increased space access and falling launch prices have stimulated the space ecosystem and exciting new space applications,” he said. The rocketry theme will also be used to inspire student interest in STEM, he added.
paras.zh: “今年的主题是火箭革命，”世界太空周协会主席丹尼斯·斯通说。他说：“它认识到太空准入的增加和发射价格的下降如何刺激了太空生态系统并令人兴奋的新太空应用。”他补充说，火箭主题还将用于激发学生对 STEM 的兴趣。

paras.en: Planned World Space Week 2026 activities include:

ESA and The Pokémon Company International will celebrate World Space Week 2026 with a Europe-wide family exhibition combining real space science with Pokémon, alongside special Pokémon GO activities at participating museums.
paras.zh: ESA 和 Pokémon Company International 将为庆祝 2026 年世界太空周举办一场欧洲范围内的家庭展览，将真实的太空科学与 Pokémon 相结合，并在参与的博物馆举办特别的 Pokémon GO 活动。

paras.en: NASA Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex will host a World Space Week Expo featuring Space Shuttle Atlantis, highlighting the Rocket Revolution and its impact on space exploration and access.

Students and rocket clubs around the world will put the Rocket Revolution into action by launching model rockets. In the U.S., enthusiasts will launch Vulcan model rockets provided by United Launch Alliance and Estes.

Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Education and SUPARCO, Pakistan’s national space agency, will lead large-scale national celebrations, with thousands of schools and events engaging students and the public in World Space Week.

UN-declared World Space Week, the largest space event on Earth, last year was celebrated by 50,000 events held by space agencies, schools, aerospace companies, and others according to the Association. World Space Week is held each October 4-10.

John Elbon, former ULA Interim CEO, serves as Honorary Chair of World Space Week 2026 to help showcase the launch industry. Tory Bruno, President of Blue Origin National Security, will serve as Honorary Chair in 2027 with the theme “To the Moon.”
paras.zh: ULA 前临时首席执行官 John Elbon 担任 2026 年世界太空周名誉主席，帮助展示发射行业。蓝色起源国家安全总裁托里·布鲁诺 (Tory Bruno) 将担任 2027 年名誉主席，主题为“To the Moon”。

paras.en: “We encourage students and the public to celebrate space in their own way next week as part of the biggest space event in the world,” Stone said. The public can see what’s planned in their area at worldspaceweek.org.

The largest space event on Earth, UN-declared World Space Week is celebrated October 4–10 annually. It is an international celebration of the contribution of space science and technology to the betterment of the human condition. World Space Week consists of numerous space-related events held by space agencies, aerospace companies, schools, planetaria, museums, astronomy clubs, and others in a common timeframe to achieve greater student and public impact through synchronization. In 2025, 50,000 events were reported in 102 countries.

World Space Week Association is the global coordinator of World Space Week. As an international non-government, non-profit organization, it serves as a permanent observer on the UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space and is supported by voluntary contributions from sponsors including Blue Origin, United Launch Alliance, Texas Instruments, Firefly Aerospace, L3 Harris, BAE Systems, Black Sky, Airbus, Club for the Future, Cesium Astro, Space Foundation, Gaia Horizons, and Space News. The Association was founded in 1982 and is one of the world’s oldest space advocacy organizations.
Dennis Stone, dstone@worldspaceweek.org (USA)
Alma Okpalefe, aokpalefe@worldspaceweek.org (Nigeria)
Ilayda Edali, iedali@worldspaceweek.org (Netherlands)

articles.title: Palestinians yearn for ‘a return to normal life,’ says top Middle East peace envoy

paras.en: Palestinians yearn for ‘a return to normal life,’ says top Middle East peace envoy
paras.zh: 中东高级和平特使表示，巴勒斯坦人渴望“恢复正常生活”

paras.en: The UN is continuing efforts to support Palestinians in Gaza amid major challenges to humanitarian access, reconstruction and the restoration of essential services, according to Ramiz Alakbarov, Acting UN Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process.
paras.zh: 联合国中东和平进程代理特别协调员拉米兹·阿拉克巴罗夫表示，在人道主义准入、重建和恢复基本服务面临重大挑战的情况下，联合国正在继续努力支持加沙的巴勒斯坦人。

paras.en: Speaking to UN News on the margins of the UN General Assembly High-Level Week, Mr. Alakbarov said UN agencies and humanitarian partners were working to address urgent needs including water, sanitation, shelter and healthcare, while also supporting efforts to remove debris, restore infrastructure and provide assistance to vulnerable communities.
paras.zh: 阿拉克巴罗夫先生在联合国大会高级别周期间接受《联合国新闻》采访时表示，联合国机构和人道主义合作伙伴正在努力解决包括水、卫生设施、住所和医疗保健在内的紧急需求，同时还支持清除废墟、恢复基础设施和向弱势社区提供援助的努力。

paras.en: Despite progress in delivering essential humanitarian assistance, significant obstacles remain, he said, including restrictions affecting humanitarian access and the entry of materials needed for reconstruction.
paras.zh: 他说，尽管在提供基本人道主义援助方面取得了进展，但仍然存在重大障碍，包括影响人道主义准入和重建所需材料入境的限制。

paras.en: Mr. Alakbarov said the needs of people in Gaza extend beyond immediate humanitarian assistance, with communities seeking better living conditions and the opportunity to rebuild their lives.
paras.zh: 阿拉克巴罗夫先生表示，加沙人民的需求不仅仅是眼前的人道主义援助，他们还寻求更好的生活条件和重建生活的机会。

paras.en: He highlighted the importance of restoring water infrastructure and medical services, supporting education and creating opportunities for people to rebuild both homes and livelihoods.
paras.zh: 他强调了恢复供水基础设施和医疗服务、支持教育以及为人们重建家园和生计创造机会的重要性。

paras.en: “One year after the ceasefire, while progress was made – on bringing such essential elements like food items, and nutrition – we still have not resolved a very cyclical matter related to water and sanitation, people don’t have access to clean water in sufficient quantities.”
paras.zh: “停火一年后，虽然在提供食品和营养等基本要素方面取得了进展，但我们仍然没有解决与水和卫生设施有关的周期性问题，人们无法获得足够数量的清洁水。”

paras.en: UN agencies, including the UN relief agency for Palestine refugees (UNRWA), continue to operate on the ground, providing a range of services and assistance, despite “the restrictions which are imposed” he said.
paras.zh: 他说，尽管“受到了限制”，包括联合国巴勒斯坦难民救济机构（近东救济工程处）在内的联合国机构仍在实地开展工作，提供一系列服务和援助。

paras.en: For Gazans, the priority is increasingly a return to normal life, including adequate shelter, access to education and the ability to rebuild homes and livelihoods, according to the UN official.
paras.zh: 联合国官员表示，对于加沙人来说，首要任务日益是恢复正常生活，包括足够的住房、接受教育以及重建家园和生计的能力。

paras.en: “Gazans are tired, they want back to normal life, they are asking to not live another winter in tents. They need better housing; they would like to work.
paras.zh: “加沙人很累，他们想要恢复正常生活，他们要求不再在帐篷里过冬。他们需要更好的住房；他们想要工作。

paras.en: “They are asking for their children to be able to go back to school. And they would like to actively contribute to the recovery of their land and to rebuilding Gaza.”
paras.zh: “他们要求自己的孩子能够重返学校。他们愿意为收复土地和重建加沙积极做出贡献。”

paras.en: Mr. Alakbarov also addressed the situation in the occupied West Bank, where he said tensions were increasing amid settler violence, economic pressures and restrictions affecting Palestinian communities.
paras.zh: 阿拉克巴罗夫还谈到了被占领西岸的局势，他表示，由于定居者暴力、经济压力和影响巴勒斯坦社区的限制，紧张局势正在加剧。

paras.en: The developments add to wider humanitarian and political concerns, with the UN continuing to call for the protection of civilians and respect for international law.
The UN continues to provide assistance, through grants that help the families reestablish their livelihoods.
paras.zh: 联合国继续提供援助，通过赠款帮助这些家庭重建生计。

paras.en: Turning to the broader political track, Mr. Alakbarov underscored continued international support for a two-State solution, with Israel and Palestine living side by side in peace and security.
paras.zh: 谈到更广泛的政治轨道，阿拉克巴罗夫先生强调国际社会继续支持以色列和巴勒斯坦和平安全共处的两国解决方案。

paras.en: He said renewed efforts were needed to rebuild trust, strengthen Palestinian institutions and create conditions for a credible political process.
paras.zh: 他表示，需要重新努力重建信任、加强巴勒斯坦机构并为可信的政治进程创造条件。

paras.en: The senior UN official's comments come as the international community continues to grapple with the humanitarian consequences of the conflict, the challenges of recovery in Gaza and growing tensions in the West Bank.
paras.zh: 联合国高级官员发表上述言论之际，国际社会仍在努力应对冲突造成的人道主义后果、加沙恢复的挑战以及西岸日益紧张的局势。

paras.en: The UN has repeatedly stressed that humanitarian assistance and recovery efforts need to be accompanied by progress towards a political settlement capable of addressing the underlying conflict.

articles.title: Ebola response faces setback as transit centre burns down in DR Congo camp

paras.en: Ebola response faces setback as transit centre burns down in DR Congo camp

The enormous challenge of halting the spread of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) just became even harder after a key transit centre for patients requiring treatment burned down in Ituri province.
Condemning the blaze, the UN’s senior Ebola response official in DRC, Julien Harneis, also noted that Kigonze camp where the facility was open now lies abandoned.
paras.zh: 联合国驻刚果民主共和国埃博拉应对高级官员朱利安·哈尼斯 (Julien Harneis) 谴责了此次火灾，他还指出，该设施所在的 Kigonze 营地现已废弃。

paras.en: “It’s been a huge struggle to create Ebola transit centres [and] Ebola treatment centres; it’s required money, bringing in staff and it’s been a struggle all across the east,” Mr. Harneis told UN News. “So, when we lose a centre, that means we lose capacity, we lose investment and we have to start again. And above all, it means that people do not get access to the care that they really need.”
The camp had provided shelter for some 19,000 people fleeing violence in the resource-rich east of the country, close to the border with Rwanda.
paras.zh: 该营地为大约 19,000 名逃离该国东部资源丰富、靠近卢旺达边境的暴力局势的人提供了住所。

paras.en: In recent days, thousands of people fled Kigonze following reports that soldiers had entered the site searching for weapons and people suspected of belonging to non-State armed groups. Gunfire was also reportedly heard.

Describing the transit centre fire on Tuesday evening as “deeply disappointing”, Mr. Harneis explained that staff there had provided “essential and excellent” services to those who needed them. He added that the UN is working with authorities to ensure that health facilities are protected.

In related developments, more than 3,000 people fled Rhoe displacement camp in Djugu territory (also in Ituri province) following clashes that intensified on 27 September. According to the UN aid coordination office, OCHA, at least four people were reportedly killed and seven injured, while several houses were burned down in Blukwa.
paras.zh: 在相关事态发展中，9 月 27 日冲突加剧后，超过 3,000 人逃离了 Djugu 地区（也在伊图里省）的 Rhoe 流离失所者营地。据联合国援助协调办公室人道协调厅称，布卢夸至少有四人死亡、七人受伤，多间房屋被烧毁。

paras.en: Women and children account for most of those displaced, according to humanitarian sources.
Fighting has also severely hampered the Ebola response and restricted humanitarian access to several health zones, including Ituri province’s Fataki, Drodro and Lita.

Ongoing insecurity has also delayed the transport of laboratory samples from Fataki to Bunia and disrupted the transfer of confirmed Ebola patients for treatment. Some aid organizations have suspended activities in affected areas.
paras.zh: 持续的不安全局势还延误了实验室样本从法塔基到布尼亚的运输，并干扰了埃博拉确诊患者的治疗转移。一些援助组织已暂停在受影响地区的活动。

paras.en: Meanwhile, in neighbouring North Kivu province, two people involved in the Ebola response were reportedly killed in Lubero on 27 and 28 September. Fighting in Masisi has displaced more than 24,000 people since mid-September.
paras.zh: 与此同时，据报道，在邻近的北基伍省，9 月 27 日至 28 日，两名参与埃博拉应对工作的人员在卢贝罗被杀。自 9 月中旬以来，马西西的战斗已导致 24,000 多人流离失所。

paras.en: OCHA and humanitarian partners are monitoring the situation and calling on all parties to protect civilians, safeguard displacement camps and ensure humanitarian access.
paras.zh: 人道协调厅和人道主义合作伙伴正在监测局势，并呼吁各方保护平民、保护流离失所者营地并确保人道主义援助准入。

paras.en: Violence has also been reported in South Kivu and Tanganyika provinces of DRC, forcing thousands more people from their homes and increasing humanitarian needs, the aid office said in an update earlier this week.

Ebola has spread across seven provinces since the public health emergency was declared in mid-May. It is the country’s 17th outbreak. The affected provinces are Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, South Ubangi and Tshopo.
paras.zh: 自5月中旬宣布公共卫生紧急状态以来，埃博拉病毒已蔓延至七个省。这是该国第 17 次爆发疫情。受影响的省份包括下韦莱省、上韦莱省、伊图里省、北基伍省、南基伍省、南乌班吉省和乔波省。

paras.en: More than 8,000 cases of infection have been confirmed including 4,000 deaths. Ituri remains the epicentre of the current emergency, with most cases in and around the cities of Bunia and Mongbwalu.
paras.zh: 已确诊超过8,000例感染病例，其中4,000人死亡。伊图里仍然是当前紧急情况的中心，大多数病例发生在布尼亚和蒙布瓦卢市及其周边地区。

paras.en: In an update, the UN World Health Organization (WHO) stressed the double challenge for Ebola responders – including safe burial teams – who urgently need more help: “Where transmission remains intense, we need to increase capacity to halt the pace of infections. And in emerging hotspots, we need to intervene quickly to stop the virus from taking hold,” the agency said.
paras.zh: 联合国世界卫生组织（WHO）在最新消息中强调了埃博拉应对人员（包括安全埋葬小组）面临的双重挑战，他们迫切需要更多帮助：“在传播仍然严重的地方，我们需要提高遏制感染速度的能力。而在新兴热点地区，我们需要迅速干预，以阻止病毒蔓延，”该机构表示。

paras.en: WHO is a key supporter of local health authorities, providing assistance with case management, surveillance, safe and dignified burials and community engagement.
paras.zh: 世卫组织是地方卫生当局的重要支持者，在病例管理、监测、安全和有尊严的埋葬以及社区参与方面提供援助。

paras.en: This is the case in Ituri’s Mongala health region, where 346 confirmed cases of Ebola have now been confirmed, with 149 deaths, since the first infection was detected on 18 May.
paras.zh: 伊图里蒙加拉卫生区就是这种情况，自 5 月 18 日发现首例感染以来，该地区现已确诊 346 例埃博拉病例，其中 149 人死亡。

paras.en: Located 45 kilometres from the provincial capital, Bunia, access remains difficult and takes nearly two hours by car. Because Mongala lacks a treatment centre, patients are either referred to Nizi – 27 kilometres away – or Bunia, depending on where beds are available and the patient’s choice.
paras.zh: 距离省会布尼亚 45 公里，交通仍然困难，需要近两个小时的车程。由于蒙加拉缺乏治疗中心，患者要么被转诊到 27 公里外的尼兹 (Nizi)，要么被转诊到布尼亚 (Bunia)，具体取决于哪里有床位以及患者的选择。

paras.en: In an update, WHO noted that the number of mobile safe and dignified burial teams has increased from 53 teams of 12 members to 114 teams deployed across Ituri province. In areas of high transmission, 57 community teams trained in safe and dignified burials were deployed across 11 health areas in Mongala and Fataki.
paras.zh: 世卫组织在最新消息中指出，部署在伊图里省的移动安全和有尊严的埋葬小组数量已从 53 个（每人 12 名）增加到 114 个。在传播率高的地区，蒙加拉和法塔基的 11 个卫生区部署了 57 个接受过安全和有尊严埋葬培训的社区小组。

paras.en: The number of patient beds has increased too, with the aim of providing more than 1,800 beds across 54 health facilities in 34 health zones. “However, more than 1,400 additional health professionals are needed to support this expansion,” the agency stressed.
paras.zh: 病床数量也有所增加，目标是在 34 个卫生区的 54 个卫生机构提供 1,800 多个床位。 “然而，还需要 1,400 多名额外的卫生专业人员来支持这一扩张，”该机构强调。

paras.en: “Increasing capacity allows us to admit more patients under better conditions and reduce delays. Rapid isolation and treatment of cases is essential,” said Dr Stéphane Mutombo, anaesthaesiologist and resuscitator, head of the clinical component within the holistic care pillar, for DRC’s Ministry of Health.
paras.zh: 刚果民主共和国卫生部麻醉师兼复苏师、整体护理支柱临床部分负责人 Stéphane Mutombo 博士表示：“容量的增加使我们能够在更好的条件下收治更多患者并减少延误。病例的快速隔离和治疗至关重要。”

paras.en: This Ebola outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus. It has become the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak in DRC, surpassing the 2018–2020 emergency.
paras.zh: 这次埃博拉疫情是由本迪布焦病毒引起的。它已成为刚果民主共和国规模最大、最致命的埃博拉疫情，超过了 2018-2020 年的紧急情况。

paras.en: It is second only to the 2014–2016 Ebola epidemic in West Africa, which infected more than 28,600 people and killed over 11,000 in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
paras.zh: 这是仅次于2014-2016年西非埃博拉疫情的第二次疫情，当时几内亚、利比里亚和塞拉利昂的埃博拉疫情导致28,600多人感染，11,000多人死亡。

articles.title: Nepal floods threaten jobs and livelihoods beyond disaster zone: ILO

paras.en: Nepal floods threaten jobs and livelihoods beyond disaster zone: ILO

The deadly flash floods in northern Nepal have severely disrupted employment and livelihoods, with wider impacts beyond communities that were directly affected, the International Labour Organization (ILO) said in a preliminary assessment released on Thursday.
“The employment consequences of this disaster will not stop at the edge of the flooded area,” said Numan Özcan, ILO Country Director for Nepal.

“Damage to transport links, electricity infrastructure and trade routes can carry the shock through supply chains, markets and connected services, affecting workers and enterprises much farther away.”

The catastrophic flooding in late August – triggered by a glacier collapse on the border with China – destroyed homes, workplaces, roads, bridges and energy infrastructure. More than 1,450 people were killed and 5,786 are still missing, according to the authorities.

The ILO estimated that some 21,400 employed people live within four kilometres of the “flood footprint”, and the disaster has disrupted economic activity and blocked workers from reaching jobs, markets and essential services.
People working in tourism, agriculture and transport and those employed by small businesses are particularly facing significant pressure.

They include guides, porters and transport operators as well as hotel, restaurant and agricultural workers. These employees may face reduced earnings, interrupted work, difficulty accessing customers, needed inputs and markets.
The ILO explained that Nepal has a high level of informal employment, meaning that many workers have limited income and social protection.
Daily-wage, casual and informal workers and those who are self-employed or who have micro- and home-based business are at heightened risk.

“Women workers may face the combined effects of lost paid work and increased unpaid care responsibilities,” the assessment said, further warning that “severe household income losses may also increase the risk of child labour as a negative coping strategy.”
The brief also examined disruption to the Nepal-China trade corridor, which could also affect companies and workers far beyond the flood-affected districts.

Two key overland routes – Rasuwa and Tatopani – accounted for some 22 per cent of Nepal’s imports from China over the past year. The floods severely damaged critical transport infrastructure in Rasuwa, responsible for nearly half of exports to China.

Disruptions “could therefore affect not only transport and border-related employment, but also workers and enterprises involved in wholesale and retail trade, construction, manufacturing, agricultural processing and other activities linked to imported inputs and export markets”.
The ILO assessment stressed that recovery and reconstruction can help protect livelihoods while creating decent employment.
It concluded with recommended next steps, including immediate income support for households and businesses, “employment-intensive reconstruction” and job matching and skills development.

articles.title: HMRC asked to explore tax implications of Man City case

paras.en: Man City charges: Treasury Committee writes to HMRC to ask about tax implications of Premier League investigation

Man City have been found guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of Premier League financial rules by an independent commission; City deny all charges and have confirmed they will appeal against the ruling and have until Friday October 2 to do so
The Treasury Committee has written to the chief executive of HM Revenue and Customs to ask about the tax implications of the Premier League's investigation into Manchester City.
HMRC could investigate whether City paid the right amount of tax and national insurance during the nine seasons they have been found guilty of financial rule breaches.

In the letter, Dame Meg Hillier MP asks JP Marks, permanent secretary of HMRC, whether the department have received an unredacted version of the Premier League's report and requests "reassurance from HMRC that you are seized of the importance of these issues and the public interest in the case".
Hillier also says she would welcome an "overview of current HMRC work around football clubs."
The letter reads: "I would be interested in any common issues around taxation (including the taxation of remuneration) that you have found in their practices, and how HMRC is tackling them."
The deadline for a reply is set at Thursday October 15, 2026.
Man City deny all allegations and plan to launch an appeal against the verdict, which they must do by Friday October 2.
- Man City reaction LIVE! Why appeal process may drag on
- Six different takes on the Man City saga by SSN reporters
- How City's 'disguised funding scheme' changed football landscape
The Premier League investigation into City was triggered by the publication of hacked internal emails in the German magazine Der Spiegel in 2018.
Der Spiegel said it had evidence which appeared to show that Roberto Mancini, who was City manager from 2009 to 2013, had a secret second contract.

As well as being paid £1.45m net by City, a company connected to him in Italy was being paid £1.75m for a four-day annual coaching consultancy commitment at Abu Dhabi-based UAE Pro League club Al Jazira.

articles.title: Britain believes Iran was involved in incident near air base used by U.S., prime minister says
articles.author: Jonathan Dienst

paras.en: LONDON — There are strong indications Tehran played a part in a security incident outside a British air base that U.S. forces use to facilitate strikes on Iran, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday.

Burnham said he had chaired an emergency security meeting this week after the incident, which happened early Sunday. Five men, all British nationals, were arrested on suspicion of terrorist and explosives offenses and were released on bail this week.
“We have been waiting to confirm what we could say, but we can now confirm our belief that Iran played a part,” he said in an interview with Sky News.
“This remains, though, a complex and very serious police investigation, so I can’t say any more at this stage,” he added.
The British Parliament is in recess, but Burnham said he “wouldn’t hesitate” to recall lawmakers “should that be necessary.”
Iran has denied any involvement in the incident.

“The embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in London categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran to arrest of five suspects in the vicinity of RAF Fairford base,” the Iranian Embassy in Britain said in a statement Monday on X.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday on X that Burnham was wrongly accusing Iran of having played a role in the incident.

“PM Burnham says the UK Government ‘can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part’ in the RAF Fairford incident,” Araghchi wrote. “I can confirm Iran’s belief that releasing supposed terrorists working for foreign states really says it all. You’re barking up the wrong tree.”
President Donald Trump told reporters Wednesday that the U.S. is closely examining the incident.
Asked whether he was planning any response to Iran, Trump replied: “Well, we are. Look, we are studying it right now. We’re studying it. We’re studying it very hard.”

“U.K. did release a number of people that we caught wanting to blow up a base,” Trump added. “We caught them early, and I’m trying to figure out if that’s for real — that they actually did it. Maybe they did it for a reason, but we’re going to know about that this afternoon, so we’ll report on that.”
In an interview with Fox News on Wednesday night, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel had provided intelligence to the U.K. about an attack.
“We gave the Brits the intel that there was going to be an attack, and it’s an Iranian-sponsored attack,” Netanyahu said, without providing additional details.
Burnham’s statements were based on intelligence that has been gathered as a result of the investigation, two senior U.S intelligence officials briefed on the matter told NBC News.
Two calls early Sunday U.K. time alerted authorities that the five people could have been up to something inappropriate, according to one official.
One call to police came from one of the five men in the group at about 12:45 a.m., the official said.
British media previously reported that call.
A local farmer called police around 1:30 a.m. local time — a call that police initially cited as the reason for the tip on the group’s activities, the official said.

No charges have been filed against the men, all in their 20s and from London, who were arrested after three vehicles were seen moving toward RAF Fairford, a British air force station about 90 minutes west of London.
Counterterrorism police later took over the case after a major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated, disrupting life in the normally quiet, rural community of the Cotswolds.
Residents were allowed to return home Monday.

In an update Tuesday, the head of counterterrorism policing, Laurence Taylor, said no explosives were found in three vans belonging to the suspects, although “a quantity of petrol” had been recovered.

“Those vehicles have been subject to extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts, and we can confirm that no improvised explosive devices were found,” he said, adding that investigators had searched properties in London.

Police in the U.K. can usually hold people for up to 24 hours before they have to charge or release them, although officers can apply to extend that time if they suspect a serious crime has been committed. Suspects arrested under the Terrorism Act can be held without charge for up to 14 days.
Trump told reporters he was disappointed by the decision to free the men on bail.
“I’m just disappointed that they caught terrorists — they did a good job, and then they sort of let them go,” he said, adding, “How do you give bail to a terrorist?”
Asked whether it was a long-standing investigation, Trump replied: “A long-standing. Yeah, we were involved in it.”
“They put them out on bail. I assume they have, they have them watched closely. But these were serious people, seriously bad people, and they should not have done that,” he added.

Burnham said Wednesday that the men were released with the “strictest possible bail conditions,” telling the BBC: “The authorities have this under the strongest grip and closest control, and I can assure you of that.”
Separately, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the incident “clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor” — an allegation British officials had not confirmed until Burnham spoke Wednesday.

Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer, gave permission for the U.S. to use its bases for “specific and limited defensive” operations against Iran. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps told the semiofficial Tasnim news agency this year that “any base used to facilitate aggression against Iranian territory is considered a legitimate target,” specifically citing bomber flights taking off from Fairford.

articles.title: U.S. ends ISIS-fighting mission in Iraq as regional security fears mount
articles.author: Helen Graham

paras.en: The last American troops assigned to fight ISIS in Iraq pulled out of the country Wednesday, ending the mission that dismantled the extremists’ self-declared caliphate but raising fears about what might fill the vacuum as the Iran war grinds on.

Though the Iraqi government welcomed the end of Operation Inherent Resolve, Kurdish officials in the north of the country said they were concerned the Biden-era decision was being carried out even after Iranian missiles pummeled them following the war launched by the United States and Israel earlier this year.

Iran-backed militias in Iraq have attacked U.S. personnel and diplomats, as well as regional allies such as Saudi Arabia. And there are fears Tehran could seek to capitalize on the U.S. withdrawal, with its proxies already celebrating the move, coupled with concerns about a potential resurgence in attacks by the remnants of the Islamic State terrorist group itself.

“We came to fight a caliphate, and there is no longer a caliphate, so we are going home,” President Donald Trump said at the White House on Wednesday, adding that the moment was a “victory for the United States,” as well as a “decisive victory over ISIS, which has been completely decimated, which is the reason we went in there in the first place.”

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said the “orderly departure” marked “the successful conclusion of the military mission that defeated ISIS in Iraq,” in a statement Wednesday. “This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region.”

The 2014 U.S.-led mission was successful in dismantling the “caliphate” ISIS governed across around 40% of Iraq and one-third of Syria, sweeping through that territory amid instability that followed the U.S. invasion and subsequent withdrawal.
But ISIS has not been defeated entirely in Iraq.

The group comprises “hundreds of fighters” across seven provincial units, according to a United Nations monitoring report in August. This “limited presence” in desert areas generates $500,000 annually through extortion of farmers and shepherds, the report said. But it is “unable to conduct significant attacks” and is only capable of “unsophisticated operations” following the killing and arrest of leaders, it said.

The U.S. expects Iraqi and Kurdish forces to now “lead the continuing effort to secure Iraq and keep ISIS remnants suppressed,” Parnell’s statement said. The Pentagon will “continue to provide targeted training and intelligence support to our Iraqi partners.”
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, who has been lavished with praise by Trump since entering office in July, described the withdrawal as the beginning of “a new phase.”

At a handover ceremony in Baghdad, he said this would be “defined by Iraq’s sovereignty, the strength of its institutions, the readiness of its forces, the unity of its decision-making and balanced partnerships with its friends.”

However, Kurdish officials, who govern the north of Iraq, expressed alarm at the move. The Kurdish Peshmerga Affairs Ministry, which oversees defense, said Monday that the U.S. leaving without establishing any other air defense was “deeply concerning.”
The withdrawal was agreed to under President Joe Biden’s administration in 2024, long before the Iran war drastically changed the region’s security landscape.

The Peshmerga Ministry said Monday that 1,000 ballistic missiles have been fired at its territory by Iran since late February. “Some have hit civilian areas, inflicting injuries, material damage and deaths,” it said, nevertheless expressing “sincere gratitude” to the U.S. and its partners “for their cooperation and support.”

The 2003 U.S.-led invasion saw around 150,000 American troops enter the country, toppling leader Saddam Hussein but also triggering a disastrous sectarian war. That combat operation came to an end in 2011, with almost all of the American personnel withdrawn.

The U.S. returned to fight ISIS in 2014, with personnel numbers peaking at almost 9,000 as of 2017. That operation wound down in 2024, and until this week only a small contingent of around 1,500 remained in the Kurdish-governed north.
After this week, a smaller contingent of U.S. forces will stay in Iraq to protect American diplomats.

Iran-backed militant groups have already celebrated the milestone as “a historic victory,” as put by Abu Mojtaba al-Yasiri, a commander in the powerful umbrella group the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, who described it as “a crushing defeat for the American project.”

And though depleted, ISIS itself “is seeking to send a message that the group is still powerful and capable of launching bloody attacks,” according to Col. Khalid al-Bayati, a senior security official in the strategic oil town of Kirkuk.

articles.title: What we know about the cockpit stabbing on Israel-bound flight
articles.author: Henry Austin

paras.en: Questions remain about how a pilot managed to sneak a weapon aboard a plane and stab his fellow pilot before it plunged thousands of feet in mere seconds. The attacker was thwarted, passengers said, and the plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
“We were so scared. We didn’t know what was going to happen,” Aviatar Alevi, a 17-year-old student, told NBC News on Wednesday after he and the rest of the passengers were flown to Tel Aviv.
Here is what we know about the incident and how close it came to resulting in tragedy.
Alevi described a harrowing scene aboard the flight, with people “screaming, running, panicking, blood.”
“At the start, I thought it was a plane malfunction, but then I started hearing screaming about the stabbings,” he said.
“We didn’t know what was going to happen,” he said, adding that the possibility of death “was definitely an option.”
Another passenger, Motti Cohen Or, 70, said that he heard a woman shouting that “someone is stabbing someone in the cockpit” before the aircraft dived “toward the ground.”
Yaniv Hayun was pictured in a bloody T-shirt telling cameras he had been among those to enter the cockpit and subdue the attacking pilot.
At Ben Gurion Airport, after the passengers had returned to Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu thanked Hayun, whom he later identified as a plumber.

Three others helped in the effort to save the plane and those aboard, Hayun told reporters. The group struggled to open the cockpit door. “I grabbed the attacker, and choked him, pulled him out first,” he said. “I started pulling the controls.”
“Thank God, we pulled it off. We really put our heads together and worked as a team,” he said. “It was between fear and a sense of a do-or-die situation.”
“We had to win. We had to pull through and come out on top,” he added.
Hailed as a hero, Indian pilot Smit Machchhar was credited by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on X for saving “the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals.”

Even though he was bleeding heavily, Machchhar managed to unlock the door to the cockpit, Netanyahu told Fox News, allowing crew members and passengers to subdue his colleague and regain control of the plane.
The Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia said in a post on X that he was admitted to hospital in Tabuk, where the plane landed, and was “reported to be in stable condition.”

According to his LinkedIn profile, Machchhar, who was also praised on social media by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, worked with India’s SpiceJet airline for more than 11 years before joining Flydubai. He has logged more than 9,750 flying hours, the profile says.

Machchhar trained as a pilot at Mainland Air in the New Zealand city of Dunedin for 18 months, beginning in 2008, the school’s CEO, Philip Kean, told the country’s 1News outlet. Machchhar “did very well” as a student and later returned to India where he worked as a recruiter for the school, Kean said.
Few details have been released about the alleged attacker, including his name and his condition.
Two senior U.S. law enforcement officials briefed on the incident told NBC News that investigators say the pilot who began stabbing the other pilot is from Oman.
Omani authorities have not commented and the Omani Foreign Ministry and the embassy in Washington did not respond to requests for comment from NBC News.

Netanyahu said the pilot was being investigated in Saudi Arabia, where he was detained after the flight landed. Netanyahu added that he believed he would eventually be taken to the United Arab Emirates.

Based on the early results of the investigation, it increasingly looks like this was an act of terrorism, a senior American official and a Saudi Arabian official briefed on the investigation told NBC News.
However, the Saudi official cautioned that the investigation was still in its early stages.
No official statements on its investigations have been released by the kingdom.

The United Arab Emirates, which owns Flydubai, is also trying to determine “whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose, or involved prior planning or direction,” the country’s state news agency reported Thursday.
Without providing any evidence, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said Wednesday that preliminary information indicated that the pilot whom he described as a terrorist aimed to crash the plane.
Netanyahu described it as “a serious security incident.”
Speaking in the Oval Office on Wednesday, President Donald Trump said he had spoken with Netanyahu “at length about this event.”
“It seems as though the co-pilot was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job, and he stabbed the pilot,” he said.
There are no indications that Iran directed or was involved in the attack, a senior U.S. official briefed on the Israeli investigation told NBC News.

And there have been no official suggestions from Israel that the Islamic Republic was behind the attack. Two Israeli security officials told The Associated Press that Israel had not identified any Iranian involvement so far.
Does this alter anything for American flights?
There are “no credible threats” to U.S. airlines, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told a news conference Wednesday.
But he said the U.S. took every incident like this very seriously “and we continue to look at the procedures that we have in place, and continue to make sure the American people are safe.”
Aside from his nationality, little is known about the pilot who carried out the attack or his motives for doing so.
Pilots undergo rigorous screening and it is standard for airlines to vet their backgrounds and check their criminal and employment history.

They also pass through metal detectors and checkpoints at airports, so it is unclear how he snuck a weapon aboard the plane. Netanyahu said in his interview with Fox News that Machchhar had apparently been stabbed or hit with an axe.
It also remains unclear whether air marshals were on board the flight at the time of the incident.

Saudi Arabia has warned that it is too early to draw definitive conclusions about who was responsible for the incident, and Israel and the UAE have announced investigations into what exactly happened on Flydubai Flight 1073.

articles.title: School and nuclear facility hit in latest wave of Russian strikes

paras.en: A nuclear facility and a school have been hit by Russian forces amid mounting air-strikes on Ukraine's capital.
The nuclear reactor at the site in Kyiv is reportedly not damaged and had been shut down since 2022.
As winter approaches, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia is targeting "critical" transmission lines which Kyiv has said is designed to cut power and heating.
Ukraine has been bombarded with high-speed 'jet-powered' attack drones, with a nuclear facility and a school hit among Russia's latest round of strikes.
The grounds of a nuclear research facility in Kyiv were hit on Wednesday, local time, causing a fire but leaving the facility's test reactor undamaged, Ukraine's nuclear safety watchdog said.

"The fire that resulted from the attack was quickly extinguished. There were no injuries," the regulator said in a statement Thursday, local time, adding that the reactor was not damaged and had been shut down since 2022.
Elsewhere in the capital, Russian drone strikes tore through a school during an air-assault on Thursday morning, local time.
Mayor Vitali Klitschko said children had been in the shelter at the moment of the strike, which sparked a fire.
The State Emergency Service released images of rescue workers picking through debris and dousing the charred building, whose windows were shattered.
The morning attack came amid intensifying, around-the-clock strikes on Kyiv and other cities with jet-powered drones which Ukraine's military has struggled to shoot down.
Earlier on Thursday, one person was wounded in a Russian air attack on a business centre in the Black Sea port city of Odesa, regional officials said.
City administration chief Serhiy Lysak said infrastructure had been damaged but gave no further details.
Odesa and the surrounding region have been a frequent target of attacks aimed partly at choking Kyiv's export revenues.
Russia, which says it strikes only military targets, reported that it had attacked a data centre in Odesa and a cargo vessel in the nearby port of Chornomorsk.
Two Russian drones hit the support section of the Southern Bridge that connects eastern and western Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital's mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
"At the moment, metro services and ground public transport across the bridge have been stopped,"
Russia has intensified its campaign of drone and missile strikes against Kyiv in recent months, putting the capital on a near-constant state of alert against attacks.
Footage shared on Telegram showed an explosion near one of the columns of the cable-stayed bridge, which carries both road traffic and trains from the Kyiv Metro.
One showed a column of thick black smoke rising into the air from the bridge, a key transport artery which crosses the Dnipro river dividing the city.
Mr Klitschko said specialists were inspecting the bridge to assess the structural damage.
Ukraine's air force said the number of Russian drone strikes on the country increased in September, with 3,177 attacks up to September 29. In August, 2,850 were recorded.
Russia has been using jet-powered attack drones that move at high speed and are harder to shoot down than the traditional models, which are based on Iranian Shaheds.
Ukraine has long feared a Russian attack on the bridges over the Dnipro, which are a lifeline for its estimated three million residents.
On Wednesday, Sergiy "Flash" Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said Russia had begun using a jet-powered drone designed to cut electricity pylons and steel bridge structures.
"I believe that the enemy is planning to attack critical high-voltage power transmission lines," he wrote on Telegram.

Russia also said on Wednesday that it had targeted Ukraine's energy infrastructure, in what Kyiv said was the opening salvo of an expected campaign designed to cut power and heating in the coming winter.

articles.title: Renee Good's family sues Trump administration over fatal Minneapolis shooting

paras.en: The family of Renee Good is suing the Trump administration over her fatal shooting at the hands of an immigration agent.
Ms Good was one of two people shot dead during a mass immigration sweep in the US city of Minneapolis, that intensified opposition to Donald Trump's migration policies.
None of the agents involved have yet faced any charges.

The family of Renee Good, one of two US citizens fatally shot by US immigration agents in Minneapolis in January, is suing US President Donald Trump's administration over her killing during deportation sweeps.

Ms Good, 37, was shot dead in her car by a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent on January 7, when she and her wife joined one of the city's daily protests against masked and armed federal agents deployed to Minnesota to arrest migrants for deportation.
The two lawsuits say Trump administration officials were negligent and violated the civil rights of Ms Good and others in Minneapolis, demanding a jury trial and damages.
"I'm here today because last January the whole world had to watch as our entire universe was destroyed," Ms Good's partner Becca Good told a press conference.
"Our government has become a grave and mortal threat to its own citizens," the family's lawyer, Antonio Romanucci said.
They are among the first major civil actions taken against Mr Trump's government for his unprecedented deportation sweeps in Minneapolis last winter, dubbed Operation Metro Surge.
Ms Good's killing intensified the backlash in Minnesota and beyond against the sweeps, involving thousands of immigration agents deployed to street patrols in Minnesota.

Days after Ms Good's death, an ICE agent shot and wounded Julio Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan delivery driver, in the leg, and two weeks later immigration agents fatally shot Alex Pretti, an American nurse working for the US Department of Veterans Affairs.
The US Supreme Court is set to also rule on whether to continue to allow the Trump administration to deny detained non-citizens the chance to seek bond.

Senior Trump administration officials initially branded Ms Good a "domestic terrorist" and the US Department of Justice stopped its federal prosecutors in Minneapolis from investigating the agents involved in her killing, prompting at least half a dozen of those prosecutors to resign in protest.
None of the agents involved has yet faced any charges.

Ms Good's killing was captured on widely viewed videos that showed the ICE agent, Jonathan Ross, approaching Ms Good in her car, which was parked to partly block the road. Mr Ross circled her car on foot, recording on his mobile.
In her last words, Ms Good can be seen on video saying to Mr Ross: "That's fine, dude, I'm not mad at you."

Moments later, another ICE agent approached the car and told Ms Good to get out. She can be seen reversing briefly, then putting the car into forward gear and turning the steering wheel to her right, apparently trying to drive away.

As the car moves forward, Mr Ross, who at that point had returned to the front left of her car, shouts "Whoa!" and shoots into the car, hitting Ms Good three times: in the head, in her arm and in her torso.

A Hennepin County investigation into the agents's conduct has been slowed because the Justice Department withdrew its usual cooperation and evidence-sharing with local law enforcement agencies. Minnesota has sued the Trump administration to gain access to the evidence it gathered at the shooting scenes.
The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE and related agencies, has defended the conduct of Ross and other immigration officers as justified uses of force in dangerous situations.

articles.title: UK-Iranian national arrested over alleged terror incident at British air base

paras.en: Counter-terrorism police arrest dual UK-Iranian national over British air base incident
Police investigating an incident at British air base RAF Fairford have arrested a dual UK-Iranian national on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts.
The 27-year-old was arrested in London and a second British man, 26, has also been questioned under caution.
The air base has been used by the US to target Iran during the recent conflict.

articles.title: This is how fast Swiss glaciers, the 'water tower of Europe,' are melting away

paras.en: This is how fast Swiss glaciers, the 'water tower of Europe,' are melting away
Water lost so far this year is 4 times Switzerland's annual consumption

Glaciers in Switzerland — the home to the most in the Alps — lost 5.5 per cent of their ice volume this year, the second-biggest percentage drop on record due to heat waves and low winter snowfall, experts report.
"Alpine glaciers have no chance of surviving in the long term under such conditions," the GLAMOS Swiss glacier monitoring service and Swiss Academy of Sciences said in a statement Thursday.
The trend has worsened in recent years. Over the past five years alone, the volume of ice in Switzerland has declined by nearly a fifth, the experts say.
The report testifies to the latest concerns that global warming is wreaking havoc on Europe, the world's fastest-warming continent.

"The warming that we are experiencing now can be attributed 100 per cent to anthropogenic climate change. It's as simple as that," said Matthias Huss, who heads GLAMOS. "Without human emissions or fossil fuels we wouldn't have any warming at the moment."

The record retreat of glacier ice in Switzerland came in 2022, when summer heat, low winter snowfall and an unusual smattering of reddish dust blown in from the Sahara darkened the glaciers and caused them to absorb more heat.
Huss said the snow cover in winter was important for two reasons.

"On the one hand, it protects the bare ice from melting. The longer you have snow, the longer you avoid the loss of old ice," said Huss in an interview at the Federal Polytechnic Institute ETHZ, where he is a glaciology professor.

"On the other hand, the snow is important also for generating new food for the glacier. The more snow you have, the higher the potential to keep some of the snow at high elevation and to form new ice."

The great thaw in Europe's legendary Alps is not alone: Experts say global warming helped to destabilize a Himalayan slope that collapsed in August and unleashed catastrophic and deadly flooding across Nepal. Satellites have shown vast shrinkage of glaciers in places like Greenland and Antarctica over the last half-century or so.

In Switzerland, in absolute terms, volume lost has been less than that in 2003, but the percentage decline this year is greater. That's because the total volume today is roughly a third of that 23 years ago. Back then, the relative loss was 3.5 per cent of total ice volume in Swiss glaciers.

Such accelerated ice melt has had an impact in Switzerland — the loss of 2.2 trillion litres from July to September amounts to four times the annual consumption of water in the country of about 9.1 million people. Switzerland gets more than half of its electricity from hydropower.
But the impact of accelerated glacier melt ripples far beyond: Switzerland is the water tower of Europe, and feeds some of the continent's most important rivers: the Danube, Po, Rhine and Rhone.

The experts say the "extreme melting" faced by Switzerland's glaciers this year included a decline in the average thickness of individual glaciers between two and half and four metres — and a reduction of up to 10 metres on the tongue of some glaciers.
The expert teams have fanned out to assess runoff and crevices caused by the running water through the glaciers, in part by dumping red dye into the streams to track the water flows.
The Allalin, Clarident, Rhone and Aletsch glaciers — Aletsch being the largest in the Alps — were among the glaciers to experience their biggest melt on record this year.
"We just need to stabilize the climate by reducing CO2 emissions and this will help the glaciers," said Huss, of GLAMOS, though he added that it is "almost too late" to save those in the Swiss Alps.

"For the ice in the polar regions like the ice sheets, there it's not yet too late," he said. "There, we can make a difference and we need to make a difference in order to limit sea level rise, for example, a factor that is a fundamental threat to billions of people living along the coast."

articles.title: What we know so far about the midair FlyDubai attack

paras.en: What we know so far about the midair FlyDubai attack
Attacked pilot recovering in hospital, Indian official says, with alleged attacker reportedly from Oman

A co-pilot stabbed his captain in an apparent attempt to crash a flight bound for Israel from the United Arab Emirates on Wednesday that was carrying 174 people. The passengers, most of them Israelis, feared for their lives as the FlyDubai aircraft lost half its altitude in about a minute.

The wounded pilot managed to open the cockpit door, and a passenger and a crew member rushed in to subdue the attacker, according to Israeli officials and plane passengers. Other crew members gained control of the aircraft, which landed safely in Saudi Arabia.
Here's what we know, and what isn't known, so far:
The distress call came at 8:44 a.m. local time, about 2½ hours after Flight FZ1073 left Dubai, a hub of international business and tourism, heading to Tel Aviv in Israel.
Israeli officials later said that the co-pilot stabbed the pilot and tried to crash the aircraft.

The plane swiftly lost altitude — dropping from 33,000 feet to 17,000 feet (10,000 metres to 5,100 metres) in the span of about a minute. It then circled close to the Jordanian border before landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, about an hour later.
Aviation experts said they were surprised that the plane did not crash after a descent so extreme that most of the rudder was ripped off the aircraft's tail.
Hours after the plane landed at Tabuk's Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport, replacement aircraft retrieved the passengers, who arrived in Israel on Wednesday night.

The wounded pilot, Capt. Smit Machchhar, from Mumbai, has been praised for opening the cockpit door so that others could subdue the attacker and take control of the Boeing 737, pulling it out of a risky dive. Other crew members were able to fly the plane to a safe landing.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on X that the pilot's opening of the cockpit door had "enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic midair disaster."

The United Arab Emirates government said an investigation team had begun its work, adding that it has jurisdiction because the plane is registered there. The state news agency said the probe will try and determine, in part, "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose, or involved prior planning or direction."

Israeli intelligence and security officials were in Saudi Arabia to help investigate the suspect, according to a regional official who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media. Israel has requested that the suspect be sent to Israel for the investigation, though it is unclear if that request will be granted, the official said.
Israeli officials have identified the attacker as an Omani national. Omani authorities have not commented.
Netanyahu said in an interview on Fox News on Thursday that the attacker had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination," but did not provide further details to support that allegation.
One question surrounding the incident is what was used in the attack — and if it was a knife, how a pilot could transport it onto the aircraft without being detected.

Pilots, like passengers, must pass through metal detectors at airports. It's also standard for airlines to check their pilots' background for criminal and employment history, and their physical and mental health, as well as having them undergo intelligence and security screening.

Netanyahu brought up the possibility in the Fox News interview that an axe was used. Airlines are generally required to carry crash axes in the cockpit for use in an emergency to break open a window to escape or break open a panel to access a fire.

The cockpit door on all aircraft is locked during flight for security reasons — a measure that became the industry standard after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, in which hijackers broke into the cockpits of four domestic flights in the United States.

Israel, targeted in a series of hijackings decades ago, has some of the most stringent airline security measures worldwide. Passengers on Israel-bound flights regularly are taken aside for questioning and baggage searches after passing through normal airport security.
Machchhar was in "good health and recovering well," the Indian Embassy in the U.A.E. said Thursday on X.
The embassy said the Indian ambassador there visited the pilot in hospital and it remained in close co-ordination with local authorities to ensure his continued medical care and well-being.
Speaking to the Times of Israel, a passenger named Dr. Shota Musaev, a dentist, said Machchhar was bleeding from the head and hands after the attack. Musaev said he helped stop the bleeding.

SpiceJet, a budget carrier in India, also praised Machchhar early Thursday. SpiceJet said he had been an employee of theirs for about a decade, with a LinkedIn profile attached to Machchhar indicating he started flying for FlyDubai in 2022.

Machchhar has logged nearly 9,750 flying hours over a career spanning about 15 years, according to a Reuters report. In a podcast interview published on YouTube last year, the captain said, "I always wanted to fly a Boeing. My first aircraft was a Boeing."

FlyDubai says it has more than 6,000 employees from 144 countries. While the airline doesn't break down those numbers by pilots, it said in 2024 that it was on a recruitment drive to hire 130 new pilots by the end of that year.

The airline, in operation for nearly 20 years, says it flies to more than 125 destinations in some 56 countries across Africa, Europe, Central Asia, the Gulf, the Middle East, the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia.

Its most tragic incident occurred in 2016, when all 62 passengers and crew aboard its Boeing 737-800 died in a nighttime crash on a second landing attempt in Russia. Pilot error was among the factors cited in the final report on the crash.
While the airline has ordered some Airbus planes for future use, its fleet at present includes dozens of Boeing 737 aircraft of various generations.
While Boeing has been under fire in the past decade regarding other aviation incidents, the American company was praised during this event by U.S. President Donald Trump on Truth Social.

"Congratulations to the GREAT Boeing company for producing a plane, the 737 Max, that was able to withstand the G Forces and Strain far beyond what it was designed and expected to. It was an amazing show of precise and powerful structural panning and design," he wrote.

articles.title: Renee Good's family sues U.S. government, ICE officer and others over Minneapolis killing

paras.en: Renee Good's family sues U.S. government, ICE officer and others over Minneapolis killing
Lawsuits allege wrongful death, conspiracy in fatal January shooting by U.S. immigration officer

Renee Good's family sued the U.S. government and several immigration officials on Thursday, alleging wrongful death, conspiracy and other violations in the 37-year-old woman's killing by an immigration officer during a federal crackdown in Minneapolis.
The two lawsuits were filed by Good's partner, Becca Good, and Renee's brother, Brent Ganger.
The U.S. Justice Department didn't immediately respond to an email seeking comment on the lawsuits.

Renee Good, a mother of three, was fatally shot Jan. 7 as protests against immigration raids flared across the city. According to Becca Good, her partner stopped their car in a street to support neighbours during an immigration operation.
- VideoRenee Good's brothers mourn loss of 'beautiful American'
- AnalysisInvestigating Renee Good's death is now up to the county — and no one else
Bystander video shows Renee Good in the driver's seat of a red SUV blocking part of the road and repeatedly honking her horn.

Two immigration officers get out of a truck, their faces covered, and one orders Good to get out of the car. She reverses briefly, then turns the steering wheel as the officer says again, "Get out of the car."
Almost simultaneously, Becca Good, standing in the street, shouts: "Drive, baby, drive!"
One officer standing in front of the vehicle pulls his weapon and fires into the windshield. He lurches back as the car turns away from him.
The officer, now very close to the open window on the driver's side, opens fire two more times, fatally shooting Renee Good, according to an analysis of the videos by The Associated Press and others.
Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defence and that Good had engaged in "an act of domestic terrorism."
Lawsuits allege wrongful death and conspiracy

The lawsuit against the United States seeks damages for Good's wrongful death and "the immense suffering Renee endured in the final moments of her life, and for the profound and permanent losses that her death has inflicted upon her family," according to a news release filed by lawyers for Becca Good and Ganger.
The lawsuit also alleges "intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligent infliction of emotional distress" on Becca Good.

Becca and Renee Good were not legally married, according to a family lawyer, but referred to one another as wives. They had only recently relocated to Minneapolis from Kansas City, Mo. It asks for a bench trial.
The other lawsuit alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights and seeks a jury trial.
- ICE nodding to far-right extremists in recruitment posts, experts say
- ICE detains 5-year-old boy coming home from Minnesota preschool

It says the shots fired by Jonathan Ross, the immigration officer who killed Good, "were the predictable and intended product of the operation," which the lawsuit describes as a "carefully planned, co-ordinated effort between senior federal officials and private actors to make two ethnic communities — Minnesotans of Somali and Hispanic descent and origin — the object of aggression and abduction, and to silence by intimidation, arrest and violence the neighbours and allies of those targeted communities who observed, documented and warned of that campaign."

The lawsuit also alleges "collaboration of federal agencies and individuals with private entities for an operation with discriminatory design, racially targeted pursuit and seizure of individuals without regard to their legal status, and each defendant's participation in the conspiracy."

It names Ross as a defendant, as well as White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security head Kristi Noem, former U.S. Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino, former campaign manager Corey Lewandowski and others.

The killing of Good and another U.S. citizen, Alex Pretti, in Minneapolis just weeks later sparked outrage across the country and calls to rein in immigration enforcement. At least 10 people have died in encounters with immigration officers during U.S. President Donald Trump's second term.

In social media accounts, Renee Good described herself as a poet, writer, wife and mom. On Pinterest, a profile picture shows her smiling and holding a young child, alongside posts about tattoos, hairstyles and home decorating.

In an interview shortly after her death, Renee Good's mother, Donna Ganger, told The Associated Press: "She had this way of making you feel special and loved that I didn't even understand … until we lost her."
"As we have tried to navigate our own massive loss, I am also devastated by how many other lives have been destroyed in this darkest of times," Becca Good said in the news release on Thursday.

"So many other families are dealing with the loss of their loved ones; to everyone who has had to witness it — the pain of this moment extends far beyond our family. What happened to us should never happen to any family."

articles.title: North and South Korea trade accusations over landmines that injured three soldiers

paras.en: Pyongyang and Seoul are trading increasingly hostile accusations across the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that divides the peninsula, 10 days after three South Korean soldiers were injured by a land mine on the South's side of the border.

The latest tensions may reflect a broader North Korean effort to test South Korea's resolve while extending its control to the outer limits of its territory, including an area that has effectively been a no-man's land for more than 70 years, according to a professor of foreign policy at South Korea's Kyung Hee University.
"The North revised its constitution in March this year and officially stated that they intend to define the absolute geographical limits of the nation, and that includes within the DMZ," said Choo.
"They want to maximize their territory and it is my sense that they would like to push the Military Demarcation Line [MDL] — the half-way point in the DMZ — further south," he told DW.
"I see the placing of landmines on the South's side of the line as a purely political act by the North, an attempt to threaten and intimidate the South."

The three men were part of an 18-strong patrol clearing a new route through the DMZ as part of an investigation into the activities of North Korean troops in the western sector of the zone. The four-kilometer-wide strip of land has divided the peninsula since the Korean War ended in an armistice in 1953.

Shortly before 11 a.m. on September 21, the patrol was around 10 meters south of the MDL when a staff sergeant detonated a mine. A second mine went off as the unit commander approached to provide assistance. Both men were successfully evacuated and have undergone surgery, with a third soldier treated for minor wounds.

The South Korean military has conducted an investigation with the United Nations Command, which administers the armistice on the border, and concluded in a report released this week that the mine was of North Korean origin.

The Joint Chiefs of Staff on Wednesday accused the North of sowing mines to the south of the MDL, a breach of the armistice agreement, and demanded an apology from Pyongyang and a commitment to halt the construction of further fortifications along the border.

"This constitutes a blatant violation of the Armistice Agreement and undermines the spirit of existing inter-Korean agreements and must be halted immediately," Kang Hyun-woo, chief director of operations, said in a press briefing.

"North Korea must immediately cease activities that heighten tensions on the Korean Peninsula, such as its so-called 'border fortification.' We strongly demand an apology and responsible measures from the North," Kang added.
In a statement, the UN Command said it had "determined that an Armistice Agreement violation occurred. UNC is addressing the violation through established Armistice mechanisms."
Many in the South are demanding more resolute action on the grounds that failure to respond will be taken as a sign of weakness in Seoul.

Na Kyung-won, a politician from the conservative opposition People Power Party (PPP), has demanded that the South Korean military carry out exercises simulating a "decapitation attack" against North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
She has also called for the restart of propaganda broadcasts from loudspeakers on the border and for dissident groups to be allowed to launch balloons carrying propaganda into the North.

Yu Yong-weon, also of the PPP, told reporters on Wednesday that North Korean troops had crossed the MDL around 20 times in August and on 30 occasions in September. On each occasion, South Korean troops fired warning shots when the incursions were detected.

An editorial in the Korea JoongAng Daily on Thursday said North Korea must be "held accountable" for the incident, arguing that Pyongyang's denial of responsibility "demands a firm response, clear accountability and stronger border enforcement."
The North is not backing down, however, with Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong Un, accusing the South of staging a provocation and threatening to retaliate.

In a statement published by the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) on Wednesday, Kim Yo Jong dismissed the South's allegations as a "self-staged farce" and accused the "South Korean armed gangs" of using the incident to justify political and military provocations against Pyongyang.
Andrei Lankov, a professor of history and international relations at Seoul's Kookmin University, is more willing to view the landmine detonations as an accident.

"It makes no sense to me for North Korea to do this deliberately," he said. "At the moment, the North wants to keep a low profile and do nothing that could provoke the South. There is no gain in a deliberate attack like this."

Lankov believes a more likely scenario is that the mines were shifted from the northern side of the MDL in heavy rain or natural movements of the terrain, meaning that the North's protestations of innocence are genuine.

"I also do not think the South Korean government has any interest in escalating the situation further and that they will hope this is quickly forgotten," he said. "They will want to brush it under the carpet."
Choo, however, is less convinced and senses a growing anger in South Korean society that the government is not standing up to provocations from north of the border.

"I believe that resuming the propaganda broadcasts over the border would be an effective response, but I do not believe this government will do that," he said. "This government is trying very hard to connect with the North, but I see a failure to take a firm line this time being interpreted in the North as a sign of weakness in Seoul.

"Not responding would give Pyongyang a green light to push a little more and then a little more again," he said. "There is a lot of anger here that the government is not doing enough to protect soldiers who are serving on the DMZ, to protect the people and to protect our territory."

articles.title: Renee Good's family sues Trump admin over fatal ICE shooting

paras.en: Relatives of Renee Good, the 37-year-old woman shot dead in her car in Minneapolis by a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent on January 7 this year, are suing the US government in a civil lawsuit connected to her death that was filed on Thursday.

Good and her wife had been taking part in daily protests in the city against the deployment of armed and often masked federal agents deployed to Minnesota to arrest and identify undocumented migrants for deportation.

The lawsuit alleges "federal conspiracy with discriminatory design and authorized use of force against observers," saying that this resulted in "extreme and unconstitutional force" being exerted against "people exercising their rights under the [US] constitution's Bill of Rights."

Good's killing, followed two weeks later by the death of nurse Alex Pretti, intensified the already-sizeable protests against the deployment of ICE and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents in Minneapolis known as Operation Metro Surge.

The plaintiffs in the twin civil suits from the Romanucci Blandin Law firm, filed on October 1, are Good's brother Brent Ganger — acting as trustee for her other next of kin including her three children — and her partner Becca Good.
One names the United States of America as the sole defendant.

The other names a series of responsible government and border control officials, including but not limited to the ICE officer who shot Good in her car, White House Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy Stephen Miller, and the US Secretary of Homeland Security at the time of the shooting, Kristi Noem.

"Renee's death was not an accident," Romanucci Blandin Law wrote in a statement. "It was the predictable result of a coordinated campaign by senior officials in this administration to target Minnesotans of Somali or Hispanic origin and silence anyone who dared to raise their voice in protest."

They allege that Operation Metro Surge "was built on exaggerated fraud accusations that the White House embraced as a pretext for thousands of masked, unidentified federal agents to rove neighborhoods and stop people based on how they looked."
It said that government officials "told agents to force confrontations with observers like Renee and led agents to believe that they would face no consequences for using force."

The crackdown in Minneapolis, which has a large Somali population, came as part of President Donald Trump's tough stance on migration and border security, and amid his assertions that local authorities in some Democrat-run states do an inadequate job fighting crime and irregular migration.
Becca Good, Renee's wife, made her public comments about the shooting at a press conference in Minneapolis on Thursday.
"I'm here today because last January the whole world had to watch as our entire universe was destroyed," she said.
Becca said of her wife: "She was pure love. She was funny. She was smart. She was gorgeous."

"Renee believed in something simple: that being good can change the world," she added. "She believed everyone deserves love and compassion, care and dignity, no matter who they were or where they came from."
Brett Ganger, Renee Good's brother, said, "The hole in my family and myself created by my sister’s passing is hauntingly apparent".

"What happened to Renee was completely senseless and the fact that there's been no accountability, no investigation, no expression of condolence, no change in policy is completely mind-blowing," Ganger said.
"What happened to America? Something must change now," he stressed.
